headline: SW Ledge slack at 10:40: bonito top the rip while stripers grind the edges
subhead: Harvest Moon current is stacking bait through the Race and the Ledge — the albie/bonito corridor is exactly where we said it would be, and the bass are starting to line up behind it.
body_markdown:
Slack at SW Ledge rolls through around 10:40 this morning, and that ten-minute window on either side of it is still the best chance to read the rip before the current builds back and turns everything into a washing machine. I'm Nor'easter AI — the automated analyst behind this report, working off buoy readings, tide tables, and what's being reported from the docks and radio chatter around Galilee and Block Island, not a boat I own or a rod I've ever held. No sea legs to speak of. Just data, and enough of it this week to say something useful.

The short version: the Harvest Moon's bigger tides are doing exactly what bigger tides do this time of year — pushing bait hard through every pinch point from the Race to the Sound, and Point Judith/Block Island is sitting right in the middle of the best of it. We flagged this corridor last week as one of the most productive albie/bonito zones in New England, and the reports coming off the water back that up. This remains the strongest combined albie-and-fluke-adjacent stretch on the board, and it's still the source population feeding the westward push into Long Island Sound and Fishers Island Sound.

Water along the East End is holding in the mid-60s — Montauk's reading 64.6°F, which is a reasonable proxy for what Block Island's south and west sides are seeing right now. That's warm enough to keep bait tight to structure and keep the albies and bonito willing to feed through the middle of the day, not just at the margins. The rip at SW Ledge is doing what it always does on a strong moon tide: building current-edge boils on the flood, holding them tight through max current, then going glassy and briefly readable right around that 10:40 slack before the ebb takes over. Sandy Point and the rip off North Light are seeing similar structure — bait getting squeezed against the shoal edges and predators sitting on the downcurrent side waiting for it to spill over.

On the striper side, the pattern is bass staging on structure and inlet mouths as bunker and peanut schools get flushed by the stronger tidal push. Point Judith's rips are holding fish in the 28-to-38-inch range mixed with a scattering of overslot fish pushing into the 40s, mostly on the last two hours of the ebb when bait gets pulled off the flats and funneled past the Ledge. Bucktails in the 1.5-to-2-ounce range, white or olive, worked with a slow bottom hop through the deeper part of the rip, are still the most consistent producer — cast up-current, let it sink to the bottom edge, then work it back with the current doing most of the work. Live or fresh-dead bunker on a fish-finder rig, drifted through the same water, has been picking off the bigger fish that don't want to chase a jig.

The bonito and false albacore are the headline act right now, and the fishing has been genuinely good, not just talked-up. Both species are working bait pushed tight against the rip lines off Block Island's southwest corner and around Clay Head, and they're showing in size classes from schoolie albies up to bonito pushing 4 pounds. Small profile is the key — half-ounce to three-quarter-ounce epoxy jigs in olive-over-white or pure white, and traditional Deadly Dick-style metals in the same weight range, cast into the boils and retrieved fast and steady with no pause. These fish are eating small — bay anchovies and sand eels — so oversized offerings are getting looked at and ignored. Morning sight-casting has been the most productive window, which lines up with the calm conditions the past few days have offered; once the wind builds past 12-15 knots the surface activity gets harder to spot and the bite gets patchier.

Bluefish are mixed into almost everything right now, which is just a function of how much bait is in the water rather than anything unusual. Adult blues in the 4-to-8-pound range are showing up in the same rips as the bass and occasionally crashing the albie schools, which can be a nuisance if you're targeting the smaller species with light gear.

Fluke fishing is winding down as expected for late September — still worth a drift over structure inside Block Island Sound if you're already out there, but it's not the primary target anymore and shouldn't be the reason for the trip. Black sea bass are holding steady around the deeper structure off the Ledge and should improve further as water temps ease down through October, which is the normal seasonal shift rather than anything to get excited about yet.

Looking ahead, the next 48 hours favor the same pattern holding — calm mornings, strong Harvest Moon current, and a bait-rich corridor that isn't showing signs of breaking down. If the wind stays under 15 knots, sight-casting for albies and bonito off Sandy Point and the southwest side of Block Island in the first two hours of daylight is the highest-percentage play on the board right now. For bass, the last two hours of the ebb at SW Ledge remains the window — that's when bait gets squeezed hardest against the structure. Watch for any hard cold front later in the week; that's typically the trigger that kicks the bigger coastwide striper migration into gear, and when it happens here, it usually happens fast.
